Aviation Incidents, field by field

Build an IXP project that reads NTSB aviation investigation reports and returns clean, structured incident data — location, aircraft, pilot, weather and probable cause. Ten stages, from an empty project to a deployed model your automations can call.

Product

UiPath IXP — Unstructured & complex documents

You will build

AviationIncidents — 5 field groups / 13 fields

Time

~25 minutes — 3 sample reports

Ends with

Deployed model — callable from RPA & API

NTSB final reports are the hard kind of document. The facts you want are scattered across nine pages of narrative prose, key–value blocks and tables, and no two reports are laid out the same way. That rules out template-based extraction and puts this squarely in IXP's Unstructured and complex documents lane, where a generative model reads the document and answers your taxonomy.

The work is mostly in the taxonomy: naming the fields you want and writing the instruction that tells the model how to find each one. Everything after that is a short loop.

01

Stage 01

Open UiPath IXP

Automation Cloud › Product launcher › IXP

  1. Sign in to Automation Cloud and open the Product launcher — the grid icon at the top-left of the shell.
  2. Scroll the rail to More and pick IXP.

IXP opens on the Projects tab with a chooser across the top. It matters which lane you are in, because each one is a different product:

  • Communications data → Communications Mining, for emails and tickets.
  • Unstructured and complex documents → Generative Extraction, for freeform text, multiple tables, graphics and inferred values. This is the lane for NTSB reports.
  • Structured and semi-structured documents → Document Understanding, for forms, invoices and purchase orders.
02

Stage 02

Create the project

Projects › Create project › Create a blank project

The dialog opens with Use Autopilot to generate project taxonomy switched on. Autopilot is a real shortcut: describe the project, drop in up to 100 pages of samples, and it drafts the field groups and fields for you.

Why turn it off here

We already know exactly which fields the downstream process needs, and the point of this guide is to show how field types and extraction instructions shape the model's answers. Authoring the taxonomy by hand makes each of those choices visible. On a real project, generating a draft with Autopilot and then correcting it is often faster.

  1. Toggle Use Autopilot to generate project taxonomy off. The primary button changes to Create a blank project.
  2. Set Project name to AviationIncidents.
  3. Click Create a blank project.
03

Stage 03

Know the workspace

AviationIncidents › Build

Spend ten seconds on this screen — every remaining stage happens on one of these three tabs.

  • Build — three cards for the working loop: Upload documents, Manage taxonomy, Validate predictions. Below them, the document list. On the right, the live Project score.
  • Measure Preview — per-field accuracy for a chosen model version, and version-to-version comparison.
  • Deploy — publish a version so automations can call it.
  • Model configuration and Manage access sit top right: choice of underlying model and pre-processing, and project roles.
04

Stage 04

Author the first field group

Build › Manage taxonomy › Fields and field groups

Open the Manage taxonomy card. An empty taxonomy explains the two building blocks and offers + Field group or Import — import takes a taxonomy file if you already have one from another project.

  • A field group is a logical set of fields, and it is also the unit that repeats. One Pilot Information group definition can produce two instances on a report that describes two pilots.
  • A field is a single data point, tied to an instance of its group.

Add the group, then the field

  1. Click + Field group. A blank row appears with the grid columns you will work in: Name, Instructions, Field type, Data type, Annotated count.
  2. Type the group name Analysis and press Enter.
  3. Click + Add underneath it to create a child field, and name it Summary.

Pick the field type — this is the important choice

New fields default to Exact Text, whose data type reads “String — exact match in the document”. The dropdown offers Boolean, Date, Exact Text, Inferred Text, Monetary Quantity, Number, plus + New field type for your own.

Exact Text vs. Inferred Text

Exact Text must be copied verbatim from somewhere in the document. Use it for identifiers, names and values printed on the page — N3KV, ERA23FA247, Lake Worth, Florida.

Inferred Text lets the model compose a value that is not written anywhere — its data type reads “can be inferred based on document”. A two-line summary of a nine-page narrative only works as Inferred Text.

Write the extraction instruction

The Instructions cell is the prompt for that one field. It is the single biggest lever you have on accuracy, and it is worth writing in plain, specific language. For Summary:

2 lines summary based on the paragraph with full details of the analysis of the event.
05

Stage 05

Complete the taxonomy

Build › Manage taxonomy › + Field group × 4

Repeat the same three moves — + Field group, name it, + Add each field — for the remaining four groups. Two conventions are worth calling out before you start.

Indented notes become instructions

In the source outline, a line nested under a field is not a sub-field — it is that field's instruction. Location → Address means one field named Location whose instruction is Address. Keeping the taxonomy flat inside each group keeps the extracted output flat too, which is what the downstream automation wants.

Two fields need a non-default type

Summary is Inferred Text, and Age is Number — its data type becomes Number rather than String. NTSB reports print the pilot's age as 77,Male, so the instruction Age (ignore sex) tells the model to return only 77. Everything else stays Exact Text.

Also on this page

Overall extraction instructions at the top applies to the whole document — a good place for context such as “this is an NTSB aviation accident final report”. Business validation checks Preview and Field types are the other two tabs, for cross-field rules and reusable custom types.

06

Stage 06

Upload sample documents

Build › Upload documents

  1. On the Build tab, use Click to browse in the Upload documents card, or drag files onto it. Accepted formats: PNG, JPG/JPEG, PDF, TIF/TIFF.
  2. Select several reports at once — here, three NTSB final reports covering different aircraft, weather and outcomes.
  3. They land in the Documents list with annotation status Not started and error rate N/A.
Choose samples deliberately

The model does not learn from document annotations. Instead, extraction results rely entirely on the taxonomy configuration and the extraction instructions defined during setup. These instructions are used by the LLM to identify and extract the required information from each document. To improve extraction quality, focus on refining the taxonomy definitions, field descriptions, and overall extraction instructions until the desired results are achieved.

Pick reports that differ in the ways that matter: single pilot vs. two pilots, day vs. night, fields that are present in one report and genuinely absent in another. Three is enough to prove the taxonomy works; it is not enough to trust an accuracy number — see stage 09.

07

Stage 07

Validate predictions

Build › Validate predictions › Document 1 of 3

Click a document name in the list (or the Validate predictions card). IXP runs the model against your taxonomy — “Generating predictions… please wait, we're analyzing the document” — then shows the document on the left and its predictions on the right, grouped exactly as your taxonomy is.

Read the prediction, then check the reference

Expand a group, then a field. Each prediction shows the extracted value and a Reference — the exact text the model grounded its answer on. The corresponding passage highlights in the document. Verifying the reference, not just the value, is what catches a plausible-but-wrong answer.

Confirm, correct, or mark missing

  • Confirm a correct prediction with the checkbox on its row. The checkbox on a group header is Confirm all extractions for that group — the fastest path when a group is entirely right.
  • Correct a wrong value with the pencil icon, or select the right text in the document. The ⊕ icon adds another occurrence of the same field.
  • Mark as missing from the row's ⋮ menu when the document genuinely does not contain the field. This is a real annotation, not a skip — it teaches the model that absence is a valid answer, which stops it inventing values.
  1. Work down every group until the counter reads all confirmed.
  2. Click Submit annotations, bottom right.
  3. The header switches to 13 Submitted and the button becomes Re-submit annotations.
“Predictions are outdated”

Change the taxonomy or any instruction and this banner appears above the panel with a Re-run predictions link. Existing predictions were produced by the old instructions, so re-run before you judge whether an instruction edit actually helped.

08

Stage 08

Finish the batch

Validate predictions › Document 2 of 3 › Document 3 of 3

Use the arrows beside Document 1 of 3 at the bottom of the panel to move through the batch without going back to the list. Each document is a fresh prediction run against the same taxonomy.

What a submission does

Each submitted document becomes training signal and produces a new project version. The Updating project… chip in the header is that work happening; when it settles to Project updated, the scores on Build and Measure reflect your latest annotations.

09

Stage 09

Measure the model

AviationIncidents › Measure Preview

Back on Build, the right rail now has numbers: a Project score with the version it was computed from, an average document error rate, and a Field performance summary with three quick filters.

Open the Measure tab for the detail: one row per field group and field, with F1 score, Error rate, Total errors, Total annotations, Annotated values, Docs with errors and Docs annotated. Pick any version from the selector, and set Comparing with to diff two versions after an instruction change.

Read the score honestly

F1 of 100 across the board is what you would expect from two annotated documents where the model already agreed with you. It says the taxonomy is coherent and the instructions are being followed; it does not say the model is production-accurate. The Annotated values < 10 filter flagging all 13 fields is the system telling you exactly that.

Keep annotating — and deliberately include the awkward reports — until each field has a few dozen annotated values. Watch Field F1 score < 50 and 50–70 for the fields that need better instructions.

10

Stage 10

Deploy the model

AviationIncidents › Deploy

The Deploy tab shows the latest project version as a card — version number, creation timestamp and the underlying model it runs on — above a Deployed versions table that starts empty. Deploying is explicit: nothing your automations call changes until you publish a version here.

  1. Click Deploy on the version card.
  2. Choose a target. To project makes the model discoverable to activities in RPA and API projects and accessible via API. To folder Preview scopes it to an Orchestrator folder instead.
  3. Add a short description — optional, but this is the changelog your teammates read in the versions table. Note what changed and why.
  4. Click Deploy.
The project is live

An RPA or API project can now call this model by name, extract the 13 fields from any NTSB-style report, and write the result to a queue, a Data Fabric entity or a downstream system. Redeploy whenever a newer version measures better; the table keeps the history so you can roll back to a known-good version.

After the tenth stage

Where this goes from here

Widen the sample set

Add reports that stress the taxonomy — missing sections, scanned pages, multiple aircraft — and annotate them. The fields with the weakest F1 are your instruction backlog.

Tune instructions, then re-run

Edit an instruction, use Re-run predictions, and compare versions on Measure. One field at a time, so you know what caused the change.

Wire it into a process

Call the deployed model from an RPA workflow, an API workflow or a Maestro flow, and add a human-in-the-loop review step for low-confidence extractions.
